terms.grammar: imperative of agō used as a particle, before another imperative; also to several people, beside agite
evidence: Plaut. Aul. 40: Exī, inquam. age exī.
terms.comment: Lewis & Short (s.v. agō): urging, “come! well! quick!”. With dum, agedum. Lewis & Short gives eja (heja) for impatient urging too: heja age, rumpe morās (Verg. A. 4.569).

terms.grammar: quīn with the present indicative, a question that urges
evidence: Plaut. Curc. 183: quīn tū īs dormītum?
Plaut. Mil. 1387: quid stās? quīn intrō īs?

phrases.english: Out, I said. Come on, out.

phrases.latin: Cedo manum, nōlō equidem tē adflīgī. — Em tenē. — Age, ī simul.
phrases.english: Give me your hand, I don’t want you to fall. — Here, hold on. — Come on, walk with me.

phrases.latin: Manē sīs videam, nē canis — — Agedum vidē.
phrases.english: Wait, let me see if there’s a dog — Go on then, look.

phrases.latin: quīn agitis hodiē? quīn datis, sī quid datis? properāte
phrases.english: come on, today! why not hand it over, if you’re handing anything? hurry up

sources: Lewis & Short: ago · Lewis & Short: quin
